title: Data Hazards & Forwarding
summary: The RAW hazard that actually shows up in an in-order pipeline, why forwarding fixes most of it, and the one case — the load-use hazard — it can't.

slides.markdown:
A **data hazard** happens when one instruction needs a value that a nearby instruction hasn't finished producing yet. In a pipeline, an instruction only writes its result back in WB — but the *next* instruction may need that value as early as its own EX stage, several cycles earlier.

**Forwarding** (also called bypassing) is the fix that closes most of this gap by routing a result directly from where it's computed back into where it's needed, skipping the slow round trip through the register file.

slides.subTitle: RAW — read-after-write
slides.markdown:
A **RAW (read-after-write)** hazard occurs when an instruction needs to *read* a register that an earlier, still-in-flight instruction hasn't *written* yet. This is the only data hazard that can actually occur in a simple in-order pipeline, because instructions read and write in the same program order they were issued in.

Example: `ADD R1, R2, R3` followed immediately by `SUB R4, R1, R5`. The SUB needs R1's new value, but ADD won't officially write R1 until its WB stage — several cycles after SUB would naively want to read it in ID.

slides.subTitle: Why WAR and WAW don't happen here
slides.markdown:
**WAR (write-after-read)** and **WAW (write-after-write)** hazards happen when instructions execute *out of program order*, so a later instruction's write could overtake an earlier read or write. In a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline, every instruction reaches every stage in strict program order — no later instruction can write before an earlier one reads or writes the same register.

These become real only once execution goes out of order — a problem register renaming solves there, not here.

slides.subTitle: A dependent pair in the pipeline
slides.markdown:
Without any fix, SUB's ID stage (where it would read R1 from the register file) happens two cycles before ADD's WB stage (where R1 actually gets written) — a clean miss.

![A dependent instruction pair showing SUB's register read landing before ADD's write-back](assets/data-hazard-raw-timing.svg)

That two-cycle gap between "needed" and "available" is exactly what forwarding closes without stalling.

assets.alt: A dependent instruction pair showing SUB's register read landing before ADD's write-back

slides.subTitle: Forwarding / bypassing
slides.markdown:
**Forwarding** adds extra wires that route a result from the pipeline register right after it's computed straight to wherever the next stage needs it — instead of waiting for that result to travel all the way through WB and back out of the register file.

Concretely: ADD computes its result in EX and it sits in the EX/MEM pipeline register at the start of the next cycle — exactly when SUB is in EX and needs it. A forwarding path feeds that value directly into SUB's ALU input that same cycle, so SUB gets the correct value with **zero stall cycles**.

slides.subTitle: Forwarding paths on the datapath
slides.markdown:
Forwarding adds muxes before the ALU inputs, letting EX select its operand from the register file, EX/MEM, or MEM/WB.

![Forwarding paths added onto the 5-stage datapath from EX/MEM and MEM/WB back into the EX stage](assets/forwarding-paths-datapath.svg)

Each cycle, logic checks whether an in-flight instruction's destination matches the current source — if so, it routes the newer value in.

assets.alt: Forwarding paths added onto the 5-stage datapath from EX/MEM and MEM/WB back into the EX stage

slides.subTitle: The load-use hazard
slides.markdown:
Forwarding assumes the needed value exists *somewhere* in the pipeline by the time it's needed. A **load** breaks this assumption: its result only becomes available at the *end* of MEM, one stage later than an ALU op's result (available at the end of EX).

If the very next instruction needs that loaded value in *its* EX stage, the value simply isn't ready yet — even forwarding straight from MEM/WB arrives one cycle too late. This is the one dependency case in a simple in-order pipeline that forwarding alone cannot eliminate; it forces exactly **one stall cycle**.

slides.subTitle: Worked load-use example
slides.markdown:
```
LW  R1, 0(R2)      ; loads R1 from memory
ADD R3, R1, R4     ; needs R1 immediately
```

```
Cycle:  1   2   3   4   5
LW:    IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
ADD:       IF  ID  --  EX  MEM WB   <- one stall (bubble) inserted
```

Without the stall, ADD's EX stage would need R1's value one cycle before LW's MEM stage produces it. Hardware detects this exact pattern (a load immediately followed by a dependent instruction) and automatically inserts one bubble, then forwards the loaded value from MEM/WB into ADD's now-delayed EX stage.

slides.subTitle: Forwarding vs NOPs vs stalling
slides.markdown:
| Approach | Who does the work | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Full forwarding | Hardware, automatically | None for ALU-to-ALU RAW hazards |
| Compiler-inserted NOPs | Compiler, at compile time | Wastes a slot the compiler could otherwise fill with useful work |
| Hardware stalling | Hardware, automatically | One bubble, but transparent to software |

Modern hardware does both: forwarding for the common case, and automatic stalling (with forwarding from the delayed value once it's ready) for the load-use case. Relying purely on the compiler to insert NOPs was an older RISC-era approach — it's simple in hardware but wastes instruction slots that a smart compiler could otherwise fill by reordering independent work into them.
